title: Typed CSV input and round-trip data contracts
outcome: Parse and export bounded CSV data using explicit types and missingness rules rather than accidental inference.
key_terms: The expected column names and element types of a file, declared up front instead of inferred from whatever rows appear.
Reading with `strict = true` so a malformed field raises an error instead of quietly becoming `missing`.
A code such as an account number that must be read as a `String`, because numeric parsing drops leading zeros.
Writing a table and reading it back to confirm that names, types and values survive serialization unchanged.
An in-memory stream that stands in for a file, so literal CSV text can be parsed without touching the disk.
approach: Write the schema before reading. Worked example A passes `types` for `id`, `amount` and `date`, `missingstring = "NA"`, a date format and `strict = true` to `CSV.read`, so every column has a declared meaning. Round trips use `CSV.write` into an `IOBuffer` and `take!` to collect the bytes, and relational checks come after parsing.

exercises.title: Preserve a textual ID
exercises.hint: Identity is not necessarily a measurement.
exercises.answer: Numeric-looking keys can lose meaning when inference converts them to integers.
exercises.why: Declaring `:id => String` keeps the text `001` exactly, so `String.(table.id)` equals `["001", "002"]`.
exercises.wrong: Letting CSV.jl infer the column type reads `001` as the integer 1, and a later join against string keys then matches nothing.
exercises.verify: Example A asserts the restored ids; print `eltype(table.id)` to see a string type rather than `Int`.

exercises.title: Declare missingness
exercises.task: Parse the authored NA amount marker.
exercises.answer: A missing marker should not silently become a valid numeric zero.
exercises.why: `missingstring = "NA"` tells the parser that `NA` means unknown, so the second amount is `missing` and the column stays `Float64` otherwise.
exercises.wrong: Replacing NA with 0 in a text editor before reading turns an absent amount into a recorded zero dollars.

exercises.title: Reject a wrong type
exercises.task: Parse 1.5 as a strict integer field.
exercises.expected: The parser raises its typed-input error.
exercises.hint: A decimal value violates this declared schema.
exercises.answer: Changing the schema or using a repair policy requires an explicit decision.
exercises.why: With `types = Int` and `strict = true`, the value `1.5` cannot be parsed as an integer, so `CSV.read` raises `CSV.Error`.
exercises.wrong: Dropping `strict = true` lets the parser substitute `missing` for the bad cell, so the schema violation becomes an apparently ordinary gap.
exercises.verify: The reference asserts `@test_throws CSV.Error` for this input and a passing strict read of `1` and `2` that sums to 3.

exercises.title: Retain quoted content
exercises.task: Round-trip a string containing a comma or quotation marks.
exercises.hint: Use the CSV writer instead of hand-concatenating fields.
exercises.answer: Correct quoting preserves structure without promising byte-identical formatting to every original file.
exercises.why: `CSV.write` quotes fields that contain the delimiter or quotation marks, so `contains,comma` and `quoted "value"` return intact.
exercises.wrong: Building lines with `join(fields, ",")` splits `contains,comma` into two columns on reread.
exercises.verify: Example B asserts `String.(restored.note) == original.note` after the round trip.

exercises.title: Handle buffer position
exercises.task: Write to an IOBuffer and then read its contents.
exercises.expected: Reset or take the bytes explicitly.
exercises.answer: An empty read after a write can reflect the current position rather than missing source data.
exercises.why: After `CSV.write(output, ...)` the buffer position sits at the end, so `take!(output)` is the call that returns all written bytes.
exercises.wrong: Calling `read(output, String)` right after writing returns an empty string, which looks like a failed export.
exercises.verify: Compare `String(take!(output))` with a fresh `read` at the end position and note which one is empty.

exercises.title: Separate parsing and meaning
exercises.task: A file parses successfully but has duplicate entity IDs.
exercises.expected: The relational data contract still needs validation.
exercises.hint: Parsing proves only part of the input boundary.
exercises.answer: Types and delimiters do not establish grain, units or scientific validity.
exercises.why: A file can parse cleanly yet contain the id `001` twice, which breaks a one-row-per-entity assumption that types cannot express.
exercises.wrong: Treating a successful `CSV.read` as full validation lets duplicate keys fan out later joins.
exercises.verify: Check `length(unique(table.id)) == nrow(table)` after parsing and report any duplicated ids.

checks_note: Parsing with `types = Int` and `strict = true` reads the two integer rows and sums them to 3, and the same settings turn `1.5` into a `CSV.Error` instead of a silent conversion. The date lines show that 2024-02-29 is a valid leap day while 2023-02-29 raises `ArgumentError`, so a declared format catches impossible dates at the boundary.
